title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
statement: Design a trie with three operations: `insert(String word)` stores a word; `search(String word)` returns true if that exact word was inserted; `startsWith(String prefix)` returns true if any inserted word begins with the given prefix.
realWorld: This class is the index behind a search box's typeahead, an IDE's completion popup, and the prefix-scan API of a key-value store. The interesting part is not `search` — a HashSet does that better — but `startsWith`, which is the operation a hash-based index cannot provide at all.

examples.explanation: The path a→p→p→l→e exists and its final node is marked terminal.
The path a→p→p exists — it is on the way to "apple" — but no word ends there, so the terminal flag is false. This single case is what the flag exists for.
`startsWith` asks only whether the path exists. It never looks at the terminal flag, which is the one line separating it from `search`.
Inserting "app" creates no new nodes — the path already exists — and only sets the flag on the node at 'p'. That flag is the entire content of the second insert.

constraints: word and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters
At most 3 * 10^4 calls in total across insert, search and startsWith

complexity.time: O(n · L) per query, i.e. O(total characters stored)

bruteForce.whySlow: Both queries re-read the entire collection, and `startsWith` compares up to L characters per word on top of that. The cost therefore grows with the dictionary, which is backwards for an autocomplete: adding a rare word should not slow down completion of a common one. With 30,000 calls against a growing list this is tens of millions of character comparisons, nearly all of them re-deciding facts an earlier query already established.

patternIdentification: The moment a problem asks for `startsWith` you are being asked to store strings in a way that preserves the relationship between similar keys — and a trie is the structure that does. The tell is that the brute force loops over every word calling `startsWith`: it re-derives, for every query, that `dog` is irrelevant to a prefix beginning with `a`. Making characters into edges means a prefix is a *position* rather than a filter, so the query becomes a walk of length L instead of a scan of size n.

optimized.idea: Make each character an edge in a tree. `insert` walks from the root, reusing an existing child when the character is already on the path and creating one otherwise — that reuse is the prefix sharing. Mark the final node terminal. `search` and `startsWith` perform the identical walk and differ by one line: `search` additionally requires the node it lands on to be terminal, `startsWith` does not care. All three are O(L) in the length of the argument, with the number of stored words appearing nowhere.

commonMistakes: Leaving out the terminal flag. After inserting only "apple", `search("app")` then returns true because the path exists. The flag is the whole difference between a stored word and a waypoint.
Checking `isWord` inside `startsWith`. That makes `startsWith("app")` false for a trie containing only "apple" — and passes any test that queries whole words, so it survives to production.
Storing the character inside the node it labels. Harmless but muddled: the character belongs on the edge, which in code means it is the key in the parent's child map. The root labels nothing.
Forgetting the null check inside the walk. `node.children.get(c)` returns null on a miss, and the next iteration dereferences it — a NullPointerException instead of a clean `false`.

Using `TrieNode[26]` without confirming the alphabet. It is the right choice for the stated lowercase-only constraint and faster than a HashMap, but it throws or silently collides the moment digits, uppercase or Unicode appear.
Building a trie when only `search` is ever called. A `HashSet<String>` is faster, far smaller and one line; the trie earns its memory only because of `startsWith`.
